title: Google Adopts Meta's Pyrefly as Its Python Type Checker, Retiring Pytype
excerpt: Google says Pyrefly delivered up to 98% faster incremental rebuilds and more than 80% compute savings across its Python monorepo, replacing the in-house Pytype after more than a decade.
body:
• Google has adopted Pyrefly, Meta's open-source Python type checker, as its standard checker across a monorepo of hundreds of thousands of Python files.
  • Google measured up to 98% faster incremental rebuilds, a 90-99% reduction in type checking on the clean-build critical path, and more than 80% savings in peak compute.
  • Pyrefly replaces Pytype, Google's own checker for more than a decade; Python 3.12 will be Pytype's final supported version.
  • For developers: Pyrefly is open source and available to try in your own projects via the Google Open Source Blog announcement, which links to the project site and repository.

Google has adopted Pyrefly, an open-source Python type checker developed by Meta, as the Python type checker across its codebase, replacing Pytype, the tool it built and used internally for more than a decade.

"Today, Pyrefly - an open source type checker developed by Meta - is the Python type checker at Google," the company said in a post on the Google Open Source Blog. Python powers everything from machine learning research to developer infrastructure and data pipelines at Google, across hundreds of thousands of files in its monorepo.

Why Pytype had to go

Pytype pioneered Python type checking and helped create typeshed, the shared repository of type stubs. Its weakness was architectural: it analysed compiled bytecode rather than source code. As Python's typing system evolved, bytecode instability across releases made keeping pace with modern typing proposals an increasing maintenance burden, and the tool struggled to deliver fast turnaround in modern development loops, Google said. The company decided Python 3.12 would be the final supported version for Pytype and evaluated open-source alternatives.

https://x.com/bitsquin/status/2111848914861367735

Why Pyrefly won

Google cited three areas. Pyrefly, written in Rust and designed for lazy, parallel evaluation, proved an order of magnitude faster than Pytype in internal benchmarks while scaling across large dependency graphs. It scores roughly 97% on the official typing conformance test suite and tracks new Python versions and typing PEPs. And it produces Rust-style diagnostics that show the offending code with inline annotations and, in some cases, suggested fixes.

The strictness difference is concrete. Pytype allowed passing a value of a union type such as int | None to a function expecting an int, as long as one type in the union was compatible. Pyrefly rejects that call and explains why: "The declared type does not allow None. Consider narrowing the value with an is not None check."

"I haven't waited for a Pytype action to complete since our project switched. It is doubly awesome for agentic coding. Type checking is faster than running the tests now."

- Peter Hawkins, JAX Tech Lead, quoted by Google

The measured gains

Google reported up to 98% faster incremental rebuilds in edit-and-rebuild workflows, with type-checking times on large machine learning targets dropping from minutes to seconds. In clean builds, Pyrefly reduced the type-checking share of the critical path by 90-99%. Daily peak compute used for Python type checking fell by more than 80%, saving thousands of machine cores a day. A secondary analysis on DEV Community summarised the same figures and noted the trade-off: static analysis can struggle with highly dynamic code that uses metaprogramming or runtime type manipulation, where bytecode analysis retained an edge.

What it signals

The move is a notable case of one technology giant standardising on a rival's developer tool - and of the Python ecosystem consolidating around shared, open-source infrastructure rather than in-house systems. For the large number of Indian engineers working in Python, at Google and elsewhere, the practical effect is faster feedback in the editor and in continuous integration, and a checker whose errors explain themselves. Google said it will keep collaborating with the Pyrefly team and contributing to the Python open-source community.
